stories.summary: Nigeria: Peace On Paper, Peril in Practice - Why 2027 Elections Remain At Risk 24 August 2026 Leadership (Abuja) By Dakuku Peterside There is reassurance in political rivals signing a common promise of peace. stories.summary: Malawi: Bitter Revolt Inside Malawi's Global Fund Body 24 August 2026 Nyasa Times (Leeds) A governance storm has erupted at the heart of Malawi's Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM) after six senior members accused officials of attempting to quietly overturn a landmark decision on who will control millions of dollars in Global Fund cash earmarked for the fight against HIV, TB and malaria. The explosive row centres on a Decisional Meeting held on Tuesday 18 August at the Ministry of Finance, where quorum was confirmed and every item on the agenda -- including the crucial selection of the Principal Recipient (PR) tasked with managing the funds -- was debated and voted on in full. But just days later, members were stunned to learn that the CCM Secretariat planned to reach out to colleagues who had been absent from the meeting, inviting them to submit "input, comments or endorsement" on the PR decision alone -- a move critics say threatens to unravel a legitimate, already-concluded vote. Six heavyweight members -- Dunker Kamba, Bishop Moffat Litchapa, Treza Mphwatiwa, Memory Kamwendo, Tionge Gondwe and Ishmael Phiri -- have now fired off a blistering letter of objection, accusing the Secretariat of trying to "manufacture participation" after the fact. It marks the latest step in an internationally brokered peace process that has seen the parties make cautious concessions, without ending the fighting. Following talks in Switzerland earlier this week, the parties have committed to "pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace", mediators said in a joint statement released on Saturday night. They staked out a roadmap "setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations" and agreed to establish a mechanism to address problems implementing the peace deal they signed late last year in Qatar, the statement said. They also affirmed "the importance of a standardised method for reporting allegations of ceasefire violations".

À lire aussi Climat: l'impact du phénomène El Niño sur l'Afrique pourrait se chiffrer à 20 milliards de dollars Ainsi, pour l'Organisation des Nations Unies pour l'alimentation et l'agriculture (FAO), la campagne agricole qui a lieu dans le pays se déroule aujourd'hui dans un contexte « de risque climatique accru, alimenté par El Niño », tandis que certains scientifiques qui étudient le phénomène dans la région estiment qu'il est étroitement lié au faible débit des eaux du Nil enregistré actuellement. Plus de 19 millions de Soudanais confrontés à une faim aiguë Résultat : quand celui-ci se manifeste à la fin du printemps comme cette année, le risque de sécheresse dans le sud-est du Soudan augmente fortement, aggravant la crise alimentaire qui y sévit en raison de la guerre qui déchire le pays depuis le mois d'avril 2023. Aujourd'hui, plus de 19 millions de Soudanais - soit plus de 40 % de la population - sont ainsi confrontés à une faim aiguë, chiffre qui fait du Soudan le théâtre de la plus grande crise humanitaire au monde en plus d'être celui qui enregistre aussi le plus grand nombre de populations déplacées sur la planète.

stories.title: Mali: libération de deux ex-paramilitaires du groupe Wagner détenus par des jihadistes et des rebelles touaregs
stories.summary: Mali: libération de deux ex-paramilitaires du groupe Wagner détenus par des jihadistes et des rebelles touaregs Détenus dans le nord du Mali, les deux hommes avaient été faits prisonniers lors des combats de Tinzaouatène, près de la frontière algérienne, en juillet 2024. Immédiatement après leur libération obtenue « grâce à l'implication de pays amis avec les juntes sahéliennes », selon une source sécuritaire malienne citée par l'AFP, ces derniers ont été conduits en Libye. Publié le : 23/08/2026 - 04:58 Modifié le : 23/08/2026 - 05:00 3 min Temps de lecture Photo non datée fournie par l'armée française de mercenaires du groupe Wagner dans le nord du Mali. © AP Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Deux ex-combattants de l'ancien groupe paramilitaire russe Wagner capturés il y a deux ans dans le nord du Mali lors de combats contre des rebelles touareg alliés à des jihadistes ont été libérés jeudi 20 août, a appris samedi l'AFP de sources sécuritaires et diplomatiques. De son côté, Africa Corps , la structure contrôlée par le gouvernement russe qui a succédé à Wagner, a confirmé vendredi 21 août la libération « de ressortissants russes détenus » depuis le 27 juillet 2024 par une « coalition terroriste FLA et Jnim [acronymes respectifs du Front de libération de l'Azawad et du Groupe de soutien à l'islam et aux musulmans, NDLR] ». Les premières images des deux ex-prisonniers montrent des hommes amaigris, l’un arborant une petite moustache, l’autre un visage mangé par une barbe.

stories.title: Les États-Unis lèvent les mesures de surveillance renforcée imposées aux navires en provenance du Nigeria
stories.summary: Les États-Unis lèvent les mesures de surveillance renforcée imposées aux navires en provenance du Nigeria En vigueur depuis 12 ans, la mesure entrainait des coûts et des délais supplémentaires pour les compagnies maritimes, ce qui pouvait les dissuader de faire escale dans les ports nigérians. Prise par Washington qui estimait à l'époque que la lutte anti-terroriste y était insuffisante, elle a pu être levée grâce à une réévaluation de la situation et à un renforcement de la coopération entre l'Administration maritime nigériane et la Garde côtière américaine. Publié le : 23/08/2026 - 04:58 2 min Temps de lecture Le port de Lagos, au Nigeria (Image d'illustration). © Sunday Alamba / AP Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Douze ans après avoir imposé des restrictions aux navires en provenance du Nigeria , les États-Unis ont annoncé mercredi 19 août leur décision de lever cette sanction. Depuis juin 2014 en effet, tout bateau ayant mouillé dans un port nigérian lors de l'une de ses cinq dernières escales avant d'arriver dans un port américain était soumis à des contrôles poussés, une mesure introduite par la Garde côtière américaine qui estimait à l'époque que la lutte anti-terroriste mise en place dans les ports nigérians étaient insuffisante, notamment en matière de contrôle des cargaisons. Grâce à un renforcement de la coopération de l'Administration maritime nigériane avec la Garde côtière américaine pour vérifier la mise en conformité de ses ports entre mars 2024 et avril 2026, ces restrictions ne vont donc plus avoir cours.

Ça fait très mal ! » Belge d'origine congolaise, Euphrasie regarde l'océan à travers la Porte du voyage sans retour par laquelle des milliers d'hommes, de femmes et d'enfants originaires d' Afrique ont été embarqués de force pour plusieurs semaines de traversée de l'Atlantique à destination des Amériques. Des hommes, des femmes et des enfants dont les souffrances se racontent chaque jour à la Maison des esclaves de Gorée, un bâtiment construit par les Français à la fin du 18e siècle, sur cette île située à seulement quelques kilomètres de Dakar, la capitale du Sénégal . « Pour ceux qui refusaient d'obéir, la punition consistait en un enfermement dans une petite cellule comme celle que vous voyez là , explique l'un des guides du site aux touristes de passage.

stories.title: Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
stories.summary: Image caption, Manasse Lomachar would like the discovery of gold to improve life in his village By Akisa Wandera Published 23 August 2026 A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks. When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; Â£205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor. And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps. It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.

stories.title: Nigeria: Jihadis kidnap dozens during Friday prayers
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JFz2 Nigerian authorities are battling several extremist groups on multiple fronts [FILE: July 31, 2026] Image: AFP Advertisement Extremists attacked and abducted a number of worshippers in Nigeria's Niger State, authorities said on Saturday. Police said the armed men attacked a number of villages in the Borgu Local Government Area before storming a mosque in the village of Kpenya during Friday prayers. "People were abducted while praying at a Juma’at mosque on Friday," Borgu area council chair Abdullahi Mohammed Nasir told the Associated Press. "That was when the bad people came and surrounded the mosque and took them away." Some witnesses recounted extreme violence. "Soon after finishing the normal Friday prayer, the armed group [...] in their hundreds, wielding guns, knives and machetes, began to attack us," one survivor told the AFP news agency. "They slaughtered some of our people, saying we are not practicing the true teachings of Islam." Local residents told the AFP and Reuters news agencies that dozens of people — as many as 60 — were kidnapped. Witnesses also told AFP that the armed men killed several people, although according to police, "the developing report indicated that no life ‌was ​lost." Who was responsible for the attack? No group claimed responsibility for the attack in the day that followed and police have not identified the culprits. One witness told AFP that the gunmen belonged to Lakurawa — an increasingly radical outfit that researchers link to the "Islamic State Sahel Province" group.

stories.summary: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, The Ashenda festival is eagerly anticipated by girls and young women in northern Ethiopia By Michael Teferi BBC Africa Published 21 August 2026 A major cultural and religious festival celebrating women and the Virgin Mary in northern Ethiopia has been cancelled in Mekelle, the main city in the Tigray region, over fears it may be targeted in drone attacks. The focal point of Ashenda festival, which traditionally draws thousands of young women dressed in their finery, was to be a mass gathering at a stadium in Mekelle on Saturday. Tigray is still recovering from a brutal two-year civil war that ended in 2022. There are concerns the conflict might reignite with the regional authorities blaming a recent series of deadly drone strikes on federal armed forces. The government has not responded to a BBC request for comment on the accusations.

stories.title: 40 years after the Lake Nyos disaster in Cameroon
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JCww The Lake Nyos incident was one of the deadliest natural disasters in Cameroon's history Image: AFP Advertisement "The Lake Nyos disaster took everybody by surprise. We had no warning signals before it ever took place," said Isaac Konfor Njilah, a Cameroonian geologist and head of a laboratory in the department of Earth Sciences at the University of Yaounde. On the night of August 21, 1986, Lake Nyos suddenly released a massive cloud of carbon dioxide that spread through nearby valleys and villages. The gas replaced oxygen, suffocating people and animals as they slept. Located in Cameroon's Northwest Region, about 315 kilometers (196 miles) northwest of Yaounde, Lake Nyos sits inside an ancient volcanic crater in the Oku volcanic field.

stories.title: Nigeria: Ahead of 2027 Elections - Youth Vote At Risk As 52% of Young Nigerians Unregistered
stories.summary: Ahead of 2027 Elections - Youth Vote At Risk As 52% of Young Nigerians Unregistered 21 August 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (Abuja) As Nigeria moves closer to the 2027 general elections, a significant number of young Nigerians may still be on the sidelines of the electoral process, with 52.1 per cent of respondents in a recent survey across 34 tertiary institutions saying they were not registered to vote. The figure rises to about 59 per cent among respondents aged 18 to 21, pointing to a major gap between Nigeria's large youth population and its participation in formal electoral processes. The findings were presented at the Next Gen YARN: "Why Youths Matter in the 2027 Elections and What Is Holding Them Back", an online intergenerational conversation hosted by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) through its Next Gen Campus Reporter Project on August 7, 2026. Respondents cited practical barriers including long queues, distance to registration centres, difficulties navigating the INEC portal, poor internet connectivity and website downtime, while distrust in the electoral system also emerged as a major concern. The survey highlighted various challenges young people faced during the recent voter registration exercise.

stories.title: 'We are devastated' - Nigerian villagers bury bodies after overloaded boat capsizes
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Crowds gathered at the bank of the river to watch the rescue mission By Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Lagos Â and Â Ruth Comerford Published 20 August 2026 Updated 21 August 2026 At least 48 people have died in Nigeria after an overloaded boat with an estimated 70 passengers capsized on a river in a remote area of north-western Sokoto state. "We are devastated at the moment," Hussaini Shehu, a resident of Gorau village, told the BBC, explaining that the accident had happened on Thursday morning as people were heading out to their rice farms along the banks of the river. Photos taken at the village mosque show many of the recovered bodies wrapped in mats and traditional cloths ahead of their burial. It is believed that so far around 10 people have been rescued. Bashir Usman Gorau, a lawmaker the area, told the BBC that many of the victims were children. In farming communities, children often accompany their parents to farms to help with agricultural activities - and at the moment the community is harvesting rice.

stories.title: Social media fueled hopes of reaching Ceuta. DW meets Moroccans caught between no future at home and the risks ahead.
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5J8kL Mother-of-two Malika believes that if she can just get to Ceuta, she will find the support she is lacking at home Image: Zhor Baki/DW Advertisement There are only a few kilometers between the city of Fnideq in Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Ceuta — but the distance between those who dream of crossing that divide and those who chose to stay in Morocco is far greater than that. After July 30, when an estimated 72,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, there were further calls on social media for people to come to Fnideq for another mass crossing attempt in mid-August. That is despite the fact that around 100 people died in the July attempt and that most of those who crossed into Ceuta have since returned to Morocco. Numbers are unclear but somewhere between 2,000 and 8,000 of those who managed to get over to the Spanish enclave remain there. According to reports, they are now living in desperate circumstances .

stories.title: Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The PDP's presidential candidate Olusegun Obasanjo swept to power in 1999, ushering in the return to democracy By Mansur Abubakar Reporting from Abuja Published 21 August 2026 Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction. A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive. A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box. It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades. For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.

stories.title: RD Congo : accord sur une feuille de route entre Kinshasa et le groupe AFC/M23
stories.summary: Publicité RD Congo : accord sur une feuille de route entre Kinshasa et le groupe AFC/M23 Afrique Réunis à huis clos en Suisse, le gouvernement de la RD Congo et le groupe rebelle AFC/M23, soutenu par le Rwanda, sont parvenus à un accord sur une feuille de route pour établir un calendrier de négociations. Ce texte s'inscrit dans le cadre du processus de Doha et fait suite à l'accord de paix parrainé par les États-Unis, fin 2023. Publié le : 23/08/2026 - 14:43 2 min Temps de lecture Partager Par : FRANCE 24 Des personnes déplacées par les combats contre les rebelles du AFC/M23 se dirigent vers le centre de Goma, en République démocratique du Congo, le 26 janvier 2025. © Moses Sawasawa, AP À l'issue de cinq jours de discussions à huis-clos en Suisse , la RD Congo et le groupe armé AFC/M23, soutenu par le Rwanda , ont trouvé samedi 22 août un accord sur une feuille de route pour guider les pourparlers de paix. Sous la médiation de la Suisse, du Qatar , des États-Unis , de l' Union africaine , et du Togo (médiateur de l'UA), les deux camps ont réaffirmé leur volonté d'appliquer l'accord-cadre de Doha signé en décembre dernier et négocié par les États-Unis . Selon un communiqué conjoint à l'issue des discussions, qui ont eu lieu du 17 au 21 août, les deux parties ont "élaboré, en collaboration avec les médiateurs, une feuille de route définissant les étapes successives et le calendrier des négociations dans le cadre de l'accord-cadre de Doha", indique le texte rendu public par les différents participants. "Elles ont réaffirmé leur engagement à poursuivre les négociations en vue d'une paix globale et d'un règlement du conflit par la mise en œuvre de l'accord-cadre ", ajoute-t-il.

stories.title: Amanal Petros: From refugee to European champion
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5J4ps Amanal Petros, seen here celebrating his gold at the European Athletics Championships, first competed for Germany at the 2021 Olympic Games Image: Stefanos Kyriazis/NurPhoto/IMAGO Advertisement Amanal Petros stood in Birmingham's Victoria Square, the German flag draped over his shoulders and the gold medal resting on his chest. Eleven months after narrowly missing out on a World Championship title in Tokyo, the 31-year-old had just won his first major marathon . After roughly 25 of the 42 kilometers, Petros picked up the pace on an incline, breaking up the lead pack. He was able to savor the victory during the final 2 kilometers. He crossed the finish line in 2:09:11 — a record time for the men's marathon at the European Athletics Championships. "My goal was to wrap things up early," Petros said afterwards. "That worked out perfectly." The fact that Italian runner Pietro Riva finished just seven seconds behind him hardly reflected the commanding nature of the victory. "I had everything under control," Petros added.

stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5J21J Wawira Njiru has been fighting for years to ensure that Kenya's schoolchildren won't be malnourished Image: Food4Education Advertisement The German Africa Foundation (DAS) is presenting the German Africa Prize to Wawira Njiru — a woman whose initiative has transformed schools meals throughout Kenya . In the beginning, Njiru started by feeding a regular meal to 25 schoolchildren; at that time, she was only a student with a dream to scale up her operation and provide a daily meal to 100 children. stories.title: How slavery reparations could help make yearning to return to Africa a reality

How slavery reparations could help make yearning to return to Africa a reality Right for people of African descent to return to continent is key pillar of global push for reparatory justice from colonisers Supporting the right for people of African descent to return to the continent has become a key pillar of the growing global push for reparatory justice from Britain and other colonisers. When Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, visited Jamaica this month he addressed the issue of repatriation for Jamaicans and others whose ancestors were kidnapped from Africa and sold into transatlantic chattel slavery. stories.title: Ebola frontline workers missing wages as outbreak spreads ‘exponentially’
stories.summary: A health worker preparing to disinfect the area during the burial of suspected Ebola victims in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters People fighting to contain rapidly growing outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo describe the obstacles and dangers they face By Prosper Heri Ngorora in Bunia and Rachel Savage E very day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo , afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends. “More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.” View image in fullscreen A health worker’s protective gear is disinfected after handling the body of a suspected Ebola victim in Bunia. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.” Ebola outbreak: five big questions Read more That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid. “I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses. Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.” View image in fullscreen A health worker dries disinfected boots in Bunia. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP U npaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.

stories.title: From former 'street kid' key to South Africa's police corruption inquiry
stories.summary: Image source, Gallo Images via Getty Images Image caption, Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala addressed some of the accusations against him when he spoke to lawmakers about corruption in the police force last year By Khanyisile Ngcobo Reporting from Johannesburg Published 15 July 2026 Updated 17 August 2026 The name of controversial businessman Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala has haunted the proceedings of South Africa's major inquiry into alleged police corruption. The 49-year-old has been accused of supplying generous gifts - including 20 impalas, the weight-loss drug Ozempic and personal loans - to help him buy influence and get police contracts. In police custody for more than a year in connection with a separate case, Matlala is giving his side of the story before retired Constitutional Court judge Mbuyiseli Madlanga and his panel after an earlier hearing last month was aborted. The revelations at the Madlanga Commission, in progress for 10 months, have gripped South Africans and they are eager to hear how Matlala responds. Dressed in a Fendi shirt and Gucci glasses, Matlala did give evidence at a parallel corruption inquiry in parliament last November.
